Moves the simulated clock forward by `duration`.

Ready tasks run as the clock passes each timer, in time order, so a task that
waits on a timer resumes at the right moment. When the call returns, the clock
reads its earlier value plus `duration`. Only available in tests.

# Panics

Panics if this executor isn't a test executor.

Lets blocking waits in tests sleep in real time when no test work can make progress.

By default, a blocking call that cannot progress panics. With parking allowed, it waits
in real time instead, and the test fails if the wait lasts 15 seconds. Use this for tests
that wait on real I/O. Undo it with [`BackgroundExecutor::forbid_parking`].

d.1:2:
In tests, run tasks until the scheduler would park.

Under the scheduler-backed test dispatcher, `tick()` will not advance the clock, so a pending
timer can keep `has_pending_tasks()` true even after all currently-runnable tasks have been
drained. To preserve the historical semantics that tests relied on (drain all work that can
make progress), we advance the clock to the next timer when no runnable tasks remain.
d.1:3:
Runs ready tasks in tests until none can make progress.

This doesn't move the simulated clock. A timer that hasn't expired stays pending,
until [`BackgroundExecutor::advance_clock`] moves time past it. Only available in
tests.

Under the scheduler-backed test dispatcher, `tick()` will not advance the clock, so a pending
timer can keep `has_pending_tasks()` true even after all currently-runnable tasks have been
drained. To preserve the historical semantics that tests relied on (drain all work that can
make progress), we advance the clock to the next timer when no runnable tasks remain.

In tests, run tasks until the scheduler would park.

Under the scheduler-backed test dispatcher, `tick()` will not advance the clock, so a pending
timer can keep `has_pending_tasks()` true even after all currently-runnable tasks have been
drained. To preserve the historical semantics that tests relied on (drain all work that can
make progress), we advance the clock to the next timer when no runnable tasks remain.

d.1:3:
Runs the future that `f` returns on a thread of its own, and returns a task for
its result.

Use this instead of [`BackgroundExecutor::spawn`] for work whose polls need more
stack than the shared background threads provide. A dedicated thread gets the
standard library's default stack of 2 MiB. Dropping the task cancels the work, as it
does for any task.
d.2:36:
Spawn a closure on a fresh session pinned to its own [`SchedulerLocalExecutor`].
The closure runs on a new OS thread under the platform scheduler, or on
the test scheduler's loop in tests.

Prefer this over [`Self::spawn`] for futures whose polls need more stack
than shared background threads guarantee. Dedicated threads get the
standard library's default 2 MiB, while `spawn` polls futures on
whatever threads the platform dispatcher provides — on macOS those are
GCD workers whose stacks are fixed at 512 KiB by the kernel (see `PTH_DEFAULT_STACKSIZE` in
<https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/libpthread/blob/42d026df5b07825070f60134b980a1ec2552dfee/kern/kern_internal.h#L154>),
the tightest background-stack budget of any platform.

the tightest background-stack budget of any platform.

d.4:5:
Dispatch a serializable request to a native process worker or browser
Web Worker and await the typed response as an executor task.

This is the portable CPU-offload path. In a browser, ordinary
[`Self::spawn`] futures are still polled on the JavaScript UI event loop;
Rust futures and closures cannot be transferred into an independently
instantiated WebAssembly worker. This method only polls the lightweight
message future on the UI loop while the registered worker handler owns
the expensive computation.
